contributions: A verifier-free selection rule for a domain where the candidates compile into an artifact whose properties can be compared directly, so agreement is measured over geometry rather than over text.

Two separately evaluated notions of agreement, geometric and topological, with the finding that each improves its own corresponding metric and the honest report that the topological one is only a tie against the verifier.

A controlled comparison on the exact candidate pools of a published verifier-based agent, with every method restricted to the same watertight subset specifically so that one variant's structural preference cannot be mistaken for selection quality.
Explicit non-comparability marking of the full-evolution reference row, which had generated additional candidates across generations while the controlled methods drew only from the initial pools.

The observation that the benefit of consensus shrinks as the generator improves -- 8 to 10 percent relative gain on weaker models against 1 to 3 percent on stronger ones -- because a stronger sampler makes a random pick a better baseline.
A closing methodological recommendation that verifiers used for candidate selection be compared against consensus selection on the same candidate pool.
limitations: Stated and unusually mechanism-specific. Consensus cannot help when all candidates are identical, and it fails outright when the same error appears in most candidates, because that error becomes the consensus -- so the method inherits whatever bias the sampler has rather than correcting it. It also favours candidates near the centre of the pool and can therefore miss a high-quality outlier, which the authors offer as part of the explanation for the persistent gap to the oracle. The geometric criterion normalises and aligns models before comparison, so absolute dimensions do not affect selection even when the prompt specifies them, and a global distance may not distinguish small local features. Comparison is at the level of the complete model rather than at feature or region level. Not stated but worth noticing: the improvements over the verifier are small in absolute terms -- 0.0017 on Chamfer distance, 0.008 on intersection-over-union -- and significant at p values between 0.003 and 0.022 on 197 prompts, so the claim is a reliable small edge rather than a large one; and the headline comparison is against one published verifier, so 'consensus beats a verifier' means this verifier on these pools.
method: Sample N parametric programs, compile each into a 3D model, and return the candidate whose compiled geometry agrees most with the rest of the pool -- selection by agreement, well established for text and code, but here measurable directly over properties of the compiled artifact rather than over strings. Two notions of agreement are defined and evaluated separately: a geometric one over normalised and aligned shapes, and a topological one over structural properties. The method is training-free and drops into existing pipelines. The evaluation is what makes the comparison readable. The verifier comparison uses the exact initial candidate populations of a published verifier-based agent, so differences come only from the selection rule. All same-pool methods -- random selection, the verifier, and both consensus variants -- select from the same watertight subset of each pool, a restriction the authors impose specifically because topological consensus would otherwise gain an advantage by inherently selecting only watertight meshes; for the verifier this means taking its highest-ranked watertight candidate, which differs from the original protocol. The published full-evolution output is reported only as a reference and explicitly flagged as not comparable, since it generates and evaluates additional candidates across multiple generations while the controlled methods select only from the initial pools. Metrics are reported on common subsets with the defined-instance count stated per metric, and coverage is defined as the percentage of prompts yielding at least one compiling candidate. The scaling study samples 1,000 candidate subsets per size, resampling any subset with no watertight candidate, and includes an oracle that picks the best candidate for the metric in question.
one_liner: Asks whether a candidate pool contains enough signal to select from itself, by compiling sampled CAD programs into 3D models and returning the one that agrees most with the rest -- and finds this verifier-free rule beats a vision-language verifier on every geometric metric when both select from the identical pool.
problem: A language model can write a parametric CAD program from a description, but a single sample is often wrong, and sampling more only helps if a good candidate can be identified -- with no ground-truth model available at generation time. Existing systems answer this with a separate verifier, typically a vision-language judge, which adds a model and a failure mode. The question the paper poses is whether that is necessary: does the candidate pool itself carry enough signal for selection.

relevance.test-time-scaling: Two things here matter beyond CAD. The first is the demonstration, under about as clean a control as this topic allows, that a learned verifier can be beaten by the pool's own agreement: both methods select from the identical candidate populations and the same watertight subset, so the difference is the selection rule and nothing else. The authors close by proposing that as a norm -- a verifier used for candidate selection should be compared against consensus selection on the same pool -- and the archive should adopt it, because it is the cheapest available null for any selection mechanism and, on the evidence here, not a weak one. It pairs directly with the archive's existing finding that a selection rule's apparent gain over majority voting can vanish under a control that merely matches the decoding format. Second, the paper is precise about when consensus works and why it fails, in terms that transfer to self-consistency generally: it cannot help when candidates are identical, it fails when the same error appears in most candidates because the error becomes the consensus, and it systematically prefers candidates near the centre of the pool and so discards high-quality outliers. That last point is the mechanism behind the persistent oracle gap and explains why agreement-based selection has a ceiling no amount of extra sampling removes -- the same asymmetry the archive holds in the finding that extra samples strengthen whatever the aggregation rule already does. The scaling-with-model-strength result is the practical one: relative gains of 8 to 10 percent on weaker generators fall to 1 to 3 percent on stronger ones, because a better sampler makes random selection a better baseline. So the value of a selection rule is inversely related to the quality of what it selects among, and a selection method demonstrated on a weak generator should be expected to shrink on a strong one. Finally, the domain is a useful reminder that agreement can be measured over the compiled artifact rather than over the text that produced it, which is a stronger signal than string matching wherever candidates execute into something comparable.

results: Selecting from identical pools, geometric consensus improves every geometric metric over the verifier -- Chamfer distance 0.0627 to 0.0610, Hausdorff 0.181 to 0.176, intersection-over-union 0.695 to 0.703, all at p at most 0.022 -- and topological consensus significantly improves two of the three (p = 0.003 and 0.035). Both consensus variants also achieve lower Chamfer distance and higher intersection-over-union than the full evolutionary pipeline, which had generated and evaluated additional candidates over multiple generations. On topology the result is a tie rather than a win: topological consensus improves over random selection (topology error 0.542 to 0.465, correctness 82.1 to 84.9 percent) but is statistically indistinguishable from the verifier (p = 0.82 and 1.00), which the authors attribute to the Euler characteristic being too coarse a signal on their data. Across four models and two prompt variants, consensus beats random selection in all eight settings, but the magnitude splits by model strength in an informative way: relative Chamfer improvement is 8 to 10 percent for the two weaker models and only 1 to 3 percent for the two stronger ones, because stronger models produce better random picks. The oracle remains clearly ahead everywhere, which by construction bounds what any selection rule over a fixed pool can achieve and locates the remaining headroom in generation.
